en: Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga Pācittiyakaṇḍa
Sappāṇakavagga 67.
The Training Rule on Arrangements.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, a certain bhikkhu was traveling from the Kosala country toward Sāvatthī and was passing through a certain village gate.
A certain woman, having quarreled with her husband, had left the village; seeing that bhikkhu, she said to him:
"Venerable sir, where is the master going?"
“I am going to Sāvatthī, sister.
“I will go with the Master,” she said.
“Come then, sister,” he replied.
Then the husband of that woman came out from the village and asked the people:
"Sirs, have you seen such a woman?
"Yes, sir, she is going along with one who has gone forth."
Then that man, having pursued and seized that bhikkhu, beat him and released him.
Then that bhikkhu sat down at the foot of a certain tree, emitting smoke.
Then that woman said this to that man:
“It is not right that this bhikkhu has defeated me;
rather, it is I who am going along with that bhikkhu;
that bhikkhu is innocent.”
“Go and ask his forgiveness.
Then that man asked the bhikkhu for forgiveness.
Thereupon, that bhikkhu went to Sāvatthī and reported this matter to the bhikkhus.
Those monks who were of few desires... they complained, grumbled, and became indignant, saying:
"How can a monk, having made an appointment with a woman, set out on a journey along a highway? ...
[and so forth] ... "Is it true, monk, that you, having made an appointment with a woman, set out on a journey along a highway?"
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked him:
“… How can you, foolish man, having made an appointment with a woman, set out on a journey along a single path?”
“Monk, this does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
And thus, monks, you should recite this training rule:
‘If any monk, having made an appointment with a woman, should travel along a highway, even as far as the next village, it is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).’”
"But whoever" means whoever of such a kind... [as previously described] ...
"a bhikkhu."
...pe... this is the meaning intended here by "a bhikkhu.
"A woman" means a human female;
not a *yakkhinī*, nor a *petī*, nor one who has gone to the animal realm—[one who is] conscious and capable of understanding what is well-spoken and ill-spoken, and what is grave and not grave.
"Together" means on one side.
"Having arranged" means—

If she makes an appointment, saying, “Let us go, sister,” “Let us go, venerable sir,” “Let us go, venerable sir,” “Let us go, sister,” or “Let us go today, or yesterday, or tomorrow,” there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
“Even as far as the interval between villages” means:
in a village where chickens can fly from one place to another, for every interval between villages, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
In an uninhabited forest, for every half-yojana, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).

If, with a woman present and perceiving her as a woman, he makes an arrangement and sets out on a journey along the same road—even if only for the distance between villages—there is an offense of expiation.

If, with a woman present but being in doubt about her, he makes an arrangement and sets out on a journey along the same road—even if only for the distance between villages—there is an offense of expiation.

If a monk, perceiving a woman as not being a woman, makes an appointment and travels along a highway with her, even if only as far as the next village, he commits an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
If the monk makes the appointment but the woman does not, he commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

If he travels along a highway with a female spirit (yakkhinī), a female ghost (petī), a paṇḍaka, or a female animal in human form, even if only as far as the next village, he commits an offense of wrong-doing.
If it is not a woman and he perceives her as a woman, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
If it is not a woman and he is doubtful, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it is not a woman and he does not perceive her as a woman, there is no offense.
There is no offense if he goes without having made an appointment;
or if the woman makes the appointment but the monk does not.
One who acts without prior agreement,
one in times of distress,
and one who is insane.
"For one who is a first-time offender.
The seventh training rule concerning making arrangements is finished.
